name: Identity Verification
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Key Proves Itself, Not the Person Behind It
lesson.summary: Identity verification is the process of binding a cryptographic key to a real-world identity, a step that authentication alone cannot provide since a key pair by itself carries no name, nationality, or legal status.
lesson.body:
Authentication, as covered earlier, proves that someone holds a specific private key. It is easy to slide from that into assuming it also proves who that someone is in the real world, a person with a name, a nationality, a legal existence. It does not. A key pair is just two large numbers mathematically related to each other; nothing about the numbers themselves says whether they belong to a bank, a teenager, or a bot. Identity verification is the separate process of establishing that link, binding a specific cryptographic key to a specific real-world entity, through some means outside the mathematics itself.

This is worth dwelling on because it is a genuinely common source of confusion. A system can be cryptographically airtight, correctly verifying signatures every single time, while telling you absolutely nothing about the real-world entity on the other end. The cryptography guarantees consistency, that the same key holder is acting each time, not identity, that the key holder is who they claim to be in the world outside the protocol. Those are different guarantees, and mistaking one for the other has caused real damage in systems that assumed a verified key was the same thing as a verified person.

This distinction has real teeth. Anyone can generate a Bitcoin key pair in seconds, entirely offline, with no registration, no application, and no oversight. That key pair can then authenticate its holder perfectly well for the purpose of spending funds sent to its address, but the network has absolutely no idea, and does not care, whether the person behind it is named Alice, is a company, or is a script running on a server somewhere. This is a deliberate design choice in permissionless blockchains, and it is genuinely useful for some purposes, but it means blockchain addresses provide authentication without identity verification, a gap that later causes real friction anywhere a legal or regulatory system needs to know an actual person is involved.

Real-world identity verification usually involves a trusted third party doing the work of checking documents and vouching for the result. A common example is Know Your Customer, or KYC, procedures at a cryptocurrency exchange: before letting someone trade, the exchange requires a government-issued ID, sometimes a selfie matched against that ID, and checks the person's name against watchlists, before linking that verified identity to an account. A notary performing an analogous role for a paper document checks a person's ID before witnessing their signature, vouching, in effect, that the signature belongs to the person it claims to.

The reason this chapter matters for what follows is that identity verification is exactly the missing ingredient that turns a bare, anonymous key pair into something a stranger can meaningfully trust. Once a trusted party has verified that a particular public key genuinely belongs to a particular, real, accountable entity, that verification can be recorded and vouched for in a durable, checkable form, rather than trusted on a one-off basis every single time. That durable, checkable record is precisely what a digital certificate is, and the trusted party that performs this verification and issues the certificate is a certificate authority, the subject of the next chapter.
